title: Leicester recorded £71m pre-tax loss for 2024-25: What would relegation to League One mean?
content:
Leicester City recorded a pre-tax loss of £71.1million ($94.6m) for the 2024-25 season, the club’s third £70m-plus loss in four years.

In a statement accompanying the release of their accounts, Leicester said the large loss was mainly due to lower player sales and the absence of non-recurring other income. That fell to just £200,000 from £12.7m in 2023-24, the latter figure comprising compensation for the departure of head coach Enzo Maresca and his staff to Chelsea, alongside the settlement of a commercial dispute.

While Leicester sold Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall for £30m to Chelsea in the summer of 2024 following promotion back to the Premier League, his sale was included in the club’s accounts for 2023-24, which recorded a loss of £19.4m. The only significant sale in 2024-25 was striker Tom Cannon to Sheffield United for £10m; player sale profits fell £64.5m, driving the more than £50m worsening of the club’s bottom line.

The club’s new chief executive Kevin Davies described the loss as “substantial” but insisted improvements to the club’s finances have been made.

With relegation to League One more plausible than a Premier League return, an ongoing reduction in income is inevitable, even as Leicester continue to receive Premier League parachute payments. Across their first-year parachute payment and distributions from the English Football League’s (EFL’s) broadcast deal, Leicester’s TV income in 2025-26 totals around £55m. It will fall to £42m next season.

A drop into the third tier would guarantee at least one year of Leicester having to make do with the TV money on offer to non-parachute clubs. Relegation after only one season in the Premier League means the club receives only two years of parachutes, so a venture to League One would confirm at least one season, in 2027-28, outside the top tier without parachute income. In the Championship, that equates to broadcast income of around £12m; in League One, it is less than £3m.

The latest accounts cover the period to June 30, 2025 and do not include player trading last summer following a return to the Championship. Leicester made a net £40.9m on player trading in the summer 2025 transfer window, though recent Companies House filings reflect the club’s need for short-term cash.

In August and September 2025 Leicester pulled forward, or ‘factored’ transfer fees due to them — in effect, paying a fee to the Australia-based Macquarie Bank, a lender, to receive the money now, rather than wait for buying clubs to pay in instalments — following the sales of Mads Hermansen, James Justin, Kasey McAteer and, though the sale occurred in January, Cannon as well. Across those deals, the club factored £30m in future transfer instalments.

Following promotion and in a bid to retain Premier League status , Leicester spent £66.9m on new signings, including attacking midfielder Bilal El Khannouss, winger Abdul Fatawu and midfielder Oliver Skipp. It came after two years of negative net transfer spending, but was insufficient to keep Leicester up.

The staff wage bill, which is predominantly made up of the players’ salaries, was £152.9m, an increase of £45.7m. That was around £40m lower than the annualised wage bill of Leicester’s 2022-23 relegation team, and on most recently available figures last season’s salary costs were the fifth-lowest in the top tier. That does still make relegation an underachievement though, especially when just 25 points were won.

Revenue for the period increased to £186.5m from £105.3m in 2023-24, driven mainly by broadcast income, which rose from £54.2m to £117.4m. Sponsorship revenue also increased from £21.5m to £37.3m, while gate receipts rose from £18.4m to £20.3m.

As a result, staff costs as a percentage of turnover improved to 82 per cent, from 102 per cent in 2023-24 and 116 per cent in the club’s previous Premier League financial period, 2022-23. While that metric moved the right way last season, TV revenue in 2025-26 has halved with a return to the Championship and will drop further next season.

Leicester’s operating loss before player sales fell to its lowest level since 2018, excluding the Covid-hit 2018-19 season. Yet at £68.6m it was still high, with no notable player sales to offset it.

“These accounts reflect the reality of returning to the Premier League,” Davies said in a statement. “Our revenues increased significantly during the year, but so too did the costs of trying to compete at that level, and the loss we are reporting is a substantial one.

“While it is natural to look first at that headline number, it is important that it is seen in its full context. The underlying operating position improved year on year as the increase in revenue was substantially larger than the increase in costs.

“We know supporters want to see Leicester City run responsibly, with the right balance between giving us the best chance of success on the pitch and building greater financial stability for the future. These financial statements show there is still more work to do, and we are clear about that.

“Improving our financial position over time remains a priority and will continue to shape the decisions we take as a club.”

Such improvements would lower Leicester’s reliance on extra funding, which remains high. The accounts confirm the club borrowed a further £50million from Macquarie in September 2024, secured against Premier League distributions. That is increasingly commonplace in football but Leicester’s scope to utilise such distributions dwindles if they spend a prolonged period out of the top tier and Premier League money payable to them tumbles.

That, plus an inability to make money from player sales or leverage external lending, would lead Leicester to even greater reliance on owners King Power International, who provided £14.3m cash last season and a further £18m in the second half of 2025. The accounts make clear both the club’s reliance on, and King Power’s commitment to, continued owner funding.

Leicester were deducted six points in February for breaching profit and sustainability rules (PSR) for the 2023-24 season, which restrict the losses a club can carry, after add-backs for investment in the club’s academy, women’s team and community work.

Premier League clubs are allowed to carry losses of £105m for a three-year cycle after add-backs. Each season in the Championship reduces the allowed losses to £13m per year.

Leicester are in the Championship relegation zone, one point from safety, with seven games remaining.

Analysis by Rob Tanner

The headline figure of another big loss will be distressing to Leicester fans already concerned about their club’s decline and its future.

In these accounts, there are at least some sprouting shoots of a recovery to some extent.

There was never going to be a quick fix for Leicester’s financial situation following the shocking relegation from the Premier League in 2022-23, when they had the seventh-largest wage bill in the league.

The loss of over £30m in prize money that season, coupled with a 116 per cent wages to turnover figure, meant the club was inevitably plunged into PSR problems as they struggled to remove high earners from their wage bill.

PSR has been looming over the club in recent years but the fall of the staff costs as a percentage of turnover to 82 per cent is a step in the right direction in lifting that shadow and was a factor in the club receiving just a six-point deduction this season when the Premier League were seeking 12 for breaches during the 2023-24 campaign.

The club are confident they can avoid another breach and comply with the regulations.

However, they carried a wage bill of £153m in the Premier League last season and, while significantly lower than previously, when it was over £200m, the squad still massively underachieved as they were relegated for the second time in three seasons.

Subsequently, more high earners have departed, which will be included in the next accounts, and more assets will be sold, regardless of whether they survive in the Championship or drop into League One for only the second time in the club’s history. The clause in El Khannouss’ loan move to Stuttgart to make it permanent has already been triggered.

As Davies has stated, there is still significant work to be done and if Leicester drop into League One their revenue streams will be further hit. They still have one more year of the Premier League’s parachute payments to come but that has already been committed to paying off a loan to Macquarie, which is factored into future accounts.

The club is still heavily reliant on its owners, the Srivaddhanaprabha family, and chairman Khun Top, and can draw on cash facilities from their company King Power International as required, but have not needed to do so far. That may change.

Losses like this one are only sustainable as long as the owners are prepared to cover them.
